title: Europa
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: A god finishes exacting a punishment and beats his wings back into the sky; his father calls him aside and, without admitting that love is the reason, sends him down to drive a king's herd to the shore of a land the natives call Sidon's, where the king's daughter plays with her Tyrian companions. Majesty and love, the poem remarks, keep bad company — and the father and ruler of the gods, whose right hand is armed with lightning, puts on the body of a bull. Snow-white, small-horned, mild-faced, he grazes and frolics until the girl dares to sit on his back. Then he walks into the sea.

advisory.lede: A god disguises himself as a bull to get close to a girl and carries her off across the sea to rape her, and the text says outright that he is only postponing “the rest”.
advisory.more: Almost the whole of this short part is charm: the white hide, the small clear horns, the harmless eye, the girl feeding him flowers and winding garlands on his horns. Ovid spends every line of the description on the disguise, then turns the whole thing over with one word — 'praedam', plunder, what a raider carries off — as the bull walks into the water with her on his back. The gap between the two registers is the point of the passage, and the last thing the poem shows is a frightened girl holding on and looking back at the shore. The rape itself falls past the end of these lines. Lectorium presents the text unaltered.

sentences.t:
Has ubi verborum poenas mentisque profanae
cepit Atlantiades, dictas a Pallade terras
linquit et ingreditur iactatis aethera pennis.
sentences.l: When he had taken these penalties for the words and for the unholy mind, Atlas's descendant leaves the lands named after Pallas and, with wings tossed, enters the upper air.
sentences.i: Having taken this payment for those words and that unholy mind, the descendant of Atlas leaves the land that carries Pallas' name and beats his wings up into the open sky.
sentences.n: 'Atlantiades' means 'the descendant of Atlas' and is the poem's name for Mercury, whose mother is Atlas's daughter; Ovid names gods by their pedigree constantly, and the glossary carries the plain name. 'Poenas ... cepit' is the ordinary idiom for exacting a punishment, with the genitives 'verborum mentisque profanae' naming what it was for — the person punished is left behind in the previous episode and never named here. 'Dictas a Pallade terras' is the country called after Pallas Athena.

sentences.t: Sevocat hunc genitor.
sentences.l: His father calls him aside.
sentences.n: 'Sevocat' is se- 'apart' plus 'voco' — the verb itself says the errand is not for other ears. 'Genitor', 'the begetter', is one of Ovid's standing words for Jupiter, and it is doing quiet work here: the father is about to send his son out on this particular business.

sentences.t:
Nec causam fassus amoris
“fide minister” ait “iussorum, nate, meorum,
pelle moram solitoque celer delabere cursu,
sentences.l: And not having confessed the cause — love — 'faithful servant,' he says, 'of my orders, son, drive off delay, and swift, glide down by your accustomed course,'
sentences.i: And without admitting that love was behind it: 'Trusty servant of my orders, my son,' he says, 'away with delay — down you go, quick, by your usual road,'
sentences.n: 'Fassus' is a deponent participle, active in sense: 'not having confessed', not 'not confessed'. The word order holds 'amoris' back to the end of the line, so the cause he is hiding is the last thing you hear. 'Delabere' is not an infinitive but the imperative of deponent 'delabor', 'glide down' — deponent imperatives in -re catch out every reader once.

sentences.t:
quaeque tuam matrem tellus a parte sinistra
suspicit (indigenae Sidonida nomine dicunt),
hanc pete,
sentences.l: and the land which looks up at your mother from the left-hand side (the natives call it Sidonian by name), make for that one,
sentences.i: and the country that looks up at your mother on its left — the people there call it Sidon's land — go there,
sentences.n: The relative clause comes before its own antecedent: 'quaeque ... tellus ... hanc pete', 'and which land ..., make for that one'. English has to turn it round. 'Tuam matrem' locates the place by the sky above it — Mercury's mother is one of the stars of the Pleiades, so the god is being given directions by constellation. 'Sidonida' keeps its Greek accusative ending; Sidon is a city of the Phoenician coast.

sentences.t:
quodque procul montano gramine pasci
armentum regale vides, ad litora verte.”
sentences.l: and the royal herd which you see feeding far off on mountain grass, turn it toward the shore.'
sentences.i: and the king's herd you can see grazing far off on the mountain grass — drive it down to the beach.'
sentences.n: 'Pasci' is an infinitive in indirect statement after 'vides' — 'you see [it] to be feeding'; the passive of 'pasco' is the normal way to say that an animal grazes. 'Armentum regale' is the local king's herd. Note what the order does and does not contain: a destination, a herd, and no reason at all.

sentences.t:
Dixit, et expulsi iamdudum monte iuvenci
litora iussa petunt, ubi magni filia regis
ludere virginibus Tyriis comitata solebat.
sentences.l: He spoke, and the bullocks, already long since driven from the mountain, make for the ordered shores, where the great king's daughter, attended by Tyrian girls, used to play.
sentences.i: He spoke; and the bullocks, driven off the mountain the instant before, are already making for the appointed shore, where the great king's daughter used to play with her Tyrian companions about her.
sentences.n: 'Iamdudum', 'long since', attached to the participle is the joke: between Jupiter's last word and the next clause the cattle are already off the mountain. Watch the tenses from here on — 'dixit' is perfect and almost everything after it is present, and that alternation runs through the whole part, Latin dropping into the present to put an action in front of you. 'Litora iussa' — 'the ordered shores' — transfers the order to the place it was about, a compression Latin makes easy and English does not. 'Magni filia regis' is a daughter identified only by her father; the poem will not give her a name anywhere in this part.

sentences.t:
Non bene conveniunt nec in una sede morantur
maiestas et amor:
sentences.l: They do not agree well, nor do they linger in one seat: majesty and love.
sentences.i: Majesty and love keep bad company, and will not stay long in one seat.
sentences.n: Both verbs arrive before you know what they are about: the subjects are held to the last two words of the clause, so the two abstractions land after they have already been described. English cannot copy that without losing the surprise. 'Sedes' is a seat or a dwelling-place, with a hint of a throne about it — which is precisely what is about to be put down. The line is a sententia, a portable maxim, dropped in as if it were common wisdom and then illustrated by a god turning himself into livestock.

sentences.t:
sceptri gravitate relicta
ille pater rectorque deum, cui dextra trisulcis
ignibus armata est, qui nutu concutit orbem,
induitur faciem tauri mixtusque iuvencis
mugit et in teneris formosus obambulat herbis.
sentences.l: with the sceptre's weight laid aside, that father and ruler of the gods, whose right hand is armed with three-forked fires, who shakes the world with a nod, puts on the form of a bull, and mixed in with the bullocks he lows and, beautiful, strolls about in the tender grass.
sentences.i: The sceptre's gravity set down, that same father and governor of the gods — the one whose right hand is armed with the three-pronged fire, who makes the world shudder at a nod — dresses himself in the shape of a bull, mixes with the bullocks, lows, and goes strolling, a handsome animal, in the soft grass.
sentences.n: 'Sceptri gravitate relicta' is an ablative absolute — a self-contained 'with X laid aside' phrase where English wants a clause. You will meet the construction constantly; 'gravitas' here is both the sceptre's weight and the dignity that comes with it, and both are being set down. 'Induitur faciem tauri' uses a passive form as a middle, 'he clothes himself in', keeping 'faciem' as its object; 'facies' is outward appearance and not the face alone, so what he puts on is the whole animal. The three grand relative clauses pile up the thunderer's credentials for four lines so that one word, 'mugit', 'he lows', can arrive at the start of the fifth.

sentences.t:
Quippe color nivis est, quam nec vestigia duri
calcavere pedis nec solvit aquaticus auster.
sentences.l: For his colour is that of snow which neither the prints of a hard foot have trampled nor the watery south wind has melted.
sentences.i: His colour is snow's — snow that no hard heel has trodden and no wet south wind has melted.
sentences.n: 'Calcavere' is '-ēre' for '-ērunt', the poetic third-person plural perfect. Verse uses it constantly and it is not a different tense from 'calcaverunt'. 'Vestigia duri ... pedis', 'the tracks of a hard foot', puts the weight on the foot rather than on whoever is walking. The whole comparison is built out of negatives — snow nothing has stepped on, snow no wind has got at — so the white is defined by what has not yet happened to it, which is an odd thing to say about a bull and a pointed thing to say in this scene.

sentences.t: Colla toris exstant, armis palearia pendent,
sentences.l: The neck stands out with muscles, from the shoulders the dewlap hangs,
sentences.i: The neck rises in ridges of muscle, the dewlap swings from the shoulders,
sentences.n: 'Colla' and 'palearia' are poetic plurals for single things — Latin verse pluralises body parts freely, and English should not follow. 'Torus' is a bulge or knot of muscle (the same word gives a stuffed couch its name); 'armus' is a shoulder, and it belongs to animals — used of a man it is rare and deliberately physical. The vocabulary has changed species along with the god. 'Palearia', the loose fold of skin under a bull's throat, is a stockman's word.

sentences.t:
cornua parva quidem, sed quae contendere possis
facta manu, puraque magis perlucida gemma.
sentences.l: the horns small indeed, but such as you could maintain were made by hand, and more translucent than a flawless gem.
sentences.i: The horns are small, true — but you would swear they had been made by hand, and they are clearer than a jewel without a flaw.
sentences.n: 'Possis' is a potential subjunctive with an indefinite 'you' — 'one could maintain', i.e. anyone would swear to it — and 'facta manu' is in indirect statement after 'contendere'. Made by hand means made by a craftsman: the animal's horns are being admired as though they were jewellery, and 'pura ... gemma' is an ablative of comparison. Magnus prints 'parva', 'small'; some editions print 'vara', 'set wide apart'.

sentences.t:
Nullae in fronte minae, nec formidabile lumen;
pacem vultus habet.
sentences.l: No threats on the brow, nor a frightening eye; his face has peace.
sentences.i: No menace in the brow, nothing to fear in the eye; the face is all peace.
sentences.n: Latin can leave out 'est' and 'sunt' altogether, and here it does so twice running; the clipped effect is part of the point, since the description is being ticked off like a buyer's inspection of an animal. 'Lumen' is literally 'light' and by extension the eye. 'Pacem vultus habet' closes a list that has spent six lines establishing one thing: that this animal is safe to walk up to.

sentences.t:
Miratur Agenore nata,
quod tam formosus, quod proelia nulla minetur.
sentences.l: Agenor's daughter marvels, because he [is] so beautiful, because he threatens no fights.
sentences.i: Agenor's daughter is taken with him — that he should be so beautiful, that there should be no fight in him at all.
sentences.n: 'Agenore nata', 'born from Agenor', is a patronymic phrase where English wants a name, and it is as close to a name as the girl gets here. Both 'quod' clauses take the subjunctive ('minetur'), which marks the reason as hers rather than the poet's: this is what she thinks, and the reader knows better. The first clause has no verb at all — the '[is]' in the literal is supplied.

sentences.t: Sed quamvis mitem metuit contingere primo:
sentences.l: But however gentle [he is], she fears to touch him at first:
sentences.i: But gentle as he is, at first she is afraid to touch him.
sentences.n: 'Quamvis mitem' is a concessive phrase with no verb of its own — 'however gentle [he may be]' — and 'mitem' is accusative because it belongs to the unexpressed object of 'contingere'; the literal supplies '[is]'. 'Primo', 'at first', quietly promises that the fear will not last, and the next line collects on the promise.

sentences.t: mox adit et flores ad candida porrigit ora.
sentences.l: soon she approaches and holds out flowers to the white mouth.
sentences.i: Soon she comes up and offers flowers to the white muzzle.
sentences.n: 'Ora' is another poetic plural for a single mouth. 'Porrigit', 'holds out, extends', is the everyday word for offering food to an animal: she is feeding it from her hand, which is where the fear ends. 'Candida', bright white, has been the keynote of this bull since the snow.

sentences.t:
Gaudet amans et, dum veniat sperata voluptas,
oscula dat manibus;
sentences.l: The lover rejoices, and, until the hoped-for pleasure should come, gives kisses to her hands;
sentences.i: The lover is delighted, and while he waits for the pleasure he is counting on, kisses her hands;
sentences.n: 'Amans', 'the lover', is what the poem calls him at this moment, and it is the first time the narration drops the disguise: the animal in the grass is named for what it wants. 'Dum' with the subjunctive 'veniat' means 'until such time as', with the waiting deliberate rather than accidental. 'Voluptas' is not a delicate word for what he is waiting for.

sentences.t: vix iam, vix cetera differt.
sentences.l: scarcely now, scarcely does he put off the rest.
sentences.i: He can hardly, hardly hold the rest of it off.
sentences.n: The doubled 'vix', 'barely', with only 'iam' between the two, makes the half-line stammer. 'Cetera', 'the remaining things', is a euphemism the reader is expected to complete, and 'differt' means 'postpones', not 'refrains from' — the difference is the whole sentence. This is where the courtship in the grass tells you what it is for.

sentences.t:
Et nunc adludit viridique exsultat in herba,
nunc latus in fulvis niveum deponit harenis;
sentences.l: And now he plays up to her and leaps about in the green grass, now he lays his snowy flank down on the tawny sands;
sentences.i: Now he frisks up to her and bounds about in the green grass, now he settles his snow-white flank on the yellow sand;
sentences.n: 'Nunc ... nunc' is 'at one moment ... at the next', the standard way of marking alternation. 'Adludit' is 'plays toward' — the prefix 'ad-' means the playing is aimed at somebody. The colours are laid on deliberately, white flank against tawny sand and green grass: this is a performance, and it is being staged for an audience of one.

sentences.t:
paulatimque metu dempto modo pectora praebet
virginea plaudenda manu, modo cornua sertis
impedienda novis.
sentences.l: and, fear little by little taken away, now he offers his chest to be patted by a maiden hand, now his horns to be tangled with fresh garlands.
sentences.i: Little by little the fear is taken away, and he offers now his chest for a girl's hand to pat, now his horns to be wound with fresh garlands.
sentences.n: 'Metu dempto' is a second ablative absolute, and Ovid does not say whose fear it is or who removed it — the impersonal phrasing quietly credits the performance rather than the girl. 'Plaudenda' and 'impedienda' are gerundives, verbal adjectives meaning 'to be patted' and 'to be entangled': he presents each part of himself already labelled with what is to be done to it. Garlands wound on the horns are also what a bull wears on the way to an altar, and the poem lets that sit there without comment.

sentences.t:
Ausa est quoque regia virgo
nescia quem premeret, tergo considere tauri,
sentences.l: The royal maiden even dared — not knowing whom she was pressing down on — to settle on the bull's back,
sentences.i: The king's daughter even dared to sit down on the bull's back, with no idea whom she was sitting on,
sentences.n: 'Nescia quem premeret' is an indirect question ('quem' plus subjunctive) governed by an adjective: 'not knowing whom she was pressing down on'. The pronoun is 'quem', 'whom', not 'quid', 'what' — the thing she cannot identify is a someone, and the reader can identify him. Here 'quoque' is the adverb 'even, also' — worth checking each time, since it is sometimes 'quō-que', 'and with which'.

sentences.t:
cum deus a terra siccoque a litore sensim
falsa pedum primis vestigia ponit in undis:
sentences.l: when the god, from the land and from the dry shore, by degrees sets the false prints of his feet in the first waves:
sentences.i: when the god, edging off the land and off the dry beach, sets his lying hoofprints in the first of the waves;
sentences.n: This 'cum' takes the indicative and inverts the sentence: the real event arrives inside the subordinate clause, a standard Latin way of springing a turn ('she had only just sat down, when ...'). 'Falsa ... vestigia' calls the tracks themselves liars, since they are a bull's and he is not one. 'Sensim', 'by degrees', is the load-bearing word — nothing happens fast enough for her to react to it.

sentences.t:
inde abit ulterius mediique per aequora ponti
fert praedam.
sentences.l: from there he goes off further, and across the level surfaces of the mid-sea he carries his plunder.
sentences.i: From there he goes further out, and across the open water of the middle sea he carries his plunder.
sentences.n: 'Praedam' is plunder, booty, what a raider carries home — and it is the poem's own word, not a character's, arriving without warning after twenty lines of a charming animal. 'Aequora' means 'the level things', the usual poetic word for the sea's flat surface, and 'medii ... ponti' is open water, out of sight of land. Two words end the courtship: he is not coaxing any more, he is carrying.

sentences.t:
Pavet haec litusque ablata relictum
respicit,
sentences.l: She is in terror, and, carried off, looks back at the shore left behind,
sentences.i: She is terrified, and, carried away, looks back at the shore she has left,
sentences.n: 'Ablata', 'having been carried off', is one passive participle doing what English needs a whole clause for — and it is also the poem's plain statement of what has happened to her. The word order interlocks: 'litus ... relictum', the abandoned shore, wraps itself around 'ablata', so the two participles sit inside one another. 'Respicit' is 'looks back', the compound holding the entire gesture.

sentences.t:
et dextra cornum tenet, altera dorso
imposita est;
sentences.l: and with her right she holds a horn, the other has been placed on his back;
sentences.i: and with her right hand she grips a horn, while the other has come to rest on his back;
sentences.n: Latin counts hands like this without naming them: 'dextra' is the right one and 'altera' the other, and the noun 'manus' never appears. 'Cornum' is a by-form of 'cornu'. The passive 'imposita est' leaves the second hand curiously agentless, as though it had been put there rather than placed by her — either way, she is holding on.

sentences.t: tremulae sinuantur flamine vestes.
sentences.l: her trembling clothes are curved by the blast.
sentences.i: Her clothes shake and belly out in the wind.
sentences.n: 'Sinuantur' comes from 'sinus', a fold or a curve, so the passive means 'are bellied out'; 'flamine' is a gust of wind, ablative of means. The part breaks off here in the middle of the crossing — the last thing the poem shows is her clothes moving, and Book II ends on the line. What becomes of her is in the next book.
